row.summaryMd: Pattern guides and full articles for the DSA roadmap. Each pattern has a short guide and, where written, an article.

blocks.body: Every design sits on the network path: client → DNS → CDN/edge → load balancer → service → data store. Know what each hop costs and what it can do for you (caching, TLS termination, routing), because latency and failure modes come from here.
A 1 by 1 pixel test image.

TCP gives an ordered, reliable byte stream with flow and congestion control, at the cost of a handshake and head-of-line blocking. UDP sends independent datagrams with no delivery guarantee; use it when late data is useless (voice, video, games) or when you build reliability yourself (QUIC).

HTTP/1.1 allows one in-flight request per connection, so browsers open ~6 connections. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection with header compression, but a lost TCP packet stalls every stream. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP), so streams are independent and connection setup is faster.

TLS 1.3 needs one round trip: the client sends supported ciphers and a key share, the server replies with its key share and certificate, and both derive symmetric keys (ECDHE). Asymmetric crypto is only used to agree on keys; bulk data uses fast symmetric encryption (AES-GCM). Resumption allows 0-RTT.

The resolver checks its cache, then asks a root server, the TLD server (.com) and the domain's authoritative server, caching each answer for its TTL. Low TTLs allow fast failover but cost more lookups; DNS can return different IPs per region (GeoDNS) to route users nearby.

A CDN caches content at edge locations close to users, cutting latency and origin load. Static assets are the obvious case; it can also cache API responses with short TTLs, terminate TLS, absorb DDoS traffic and run edge logic. Invalidate by versioned URLs rather than purges where possible.

L4 balancers route by IP and port without reading the payload: very fast, protocol-agnostic. L7 balancers parse HTTP, so they can route by path or header, terminate TLS, retry, and do sticky sessions. Common algorithms: round robin, least connections, consistent hashing (for cache affinity).

A forward proxy acts for clients (corporate egress, anonymity). A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and acts for them: TLS termination, compression, caching, rate limiting, routing to backends. Nginx, Envoy and HAProxy are typical; an API gateway is a reverse proxy with auth and API-level policies.
Request path: DNS → CDN/edge → L4/L7 load balancer → service → cache/DB.
TCP handshake 1 RTT + TLS 1.3 1 RTT before the first byte; reuse connections.
HTTP/2 multiplexes but suffers TCP head-of-line blocking; HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP) fixes it.
L4 = fast, protocol-agnostic; L7 = route by path/header, TLS termination, retries.

sections.title: Worked example: what a cold request costs

blocks.body:
User in Mumbai, origin in us-east (≈200 ms RTT). Cold: DNS lookup (cache miss, ~50-100 ms), TCP handshake (1 RTT = 200 ms), TLS 1.3 (1 RTT = 200 ms), request + response (1 RTT = 200 ms) → ~650 ms before any server time.

With a CDN PoP in Mumbai (≈10 ms RTT) terminating TLS and keeping warm connections to the origin: handshakes cost ~20 ms, and cached content returns in ~30 ms total. That's why designs put TLS termination and caching at the edge, and why connection reuse (keep-alive, HTTP/2) matters more than raw bandwidth.

TCP turns an unreliable packet network into a reliable, ordered byte stream. The handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) agrees on starting sequence numbers. Every byte has a sequence number; the receiver acknowledges what it has received in order (cumulative ACKs), and the sender retransmits anything not acknowledged in time or after three duplicate ACKs (fast retransmit). Flow control uses the receiver's advertised window so a fast sender can't overflow a slow receiver; congestion control (slow start, then additive increase / multiplicative decrease, or BBR) keeps the sender from overwhelming the network.

The costs: one round trip before any data, head-of-line blocking (a lost segment holds back everything after it, even data for unrelated requests), and per-connection state in the kernel. That's why connection reuse matters and why HTTP/3 moved to QUIC.

UDP sends independent datagrams with an 8-byte header: no handshake, no ordering, no retransmission, no congestion control. The application decides what to do with loss. It fits DNS (one small question, one small answer, retry on timeout), real-time media (a late voice packet is worthless), games (send the latest state, ignore old), and protocols that build their own reliability (QUIC, many VPNs). In a design, say UDP only when late data is useless or you're consciously re-implementing reliability.

sections.title: HTTP versions and what they change for a system

blocks.body:
HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive but serves one request at a time per connection (pipelining exists but is effectively unused), so browsers open about 6 connections per host and developers used tricks like domain sharding and sprite sheets. Each response is text headers plus a body; headers repeat on every request.

HTTP/2 is binary and multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, with HPACK header compression and stream priorities. One connection per host is enough, which reduces handshakes and helps TLS and congestion windows warm up. Its weakness is TCP: a single lost packet stalls every stream on the connection, which hurts on lossy mobile networks. gRPC is built on HTTP/2 and uses its streaming.

HTTP/3 runs HTTP over QUIC on UDP. Streams are independent at the transport level, so loss on one doesn't block the others; the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes are combined (1 RTT, 0-RTT on resumption); and connections survive IP changes (Wi-Fi to cellular) because they're identified by connection IDs. The cost is more CPU in user space and some networks that block or throttle UDP, so clients fall back to HTTP/2.

For a design answer: terminate HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 at the edge (CDN or load balancer) for clients, and use HTTP/2 or gRPC with long-lived pooled connections between internal services.

sections.title: CDNs, proxies and gateways: what sits where

blocks.body:
A CDN is a network of edge servers (PoPs) near users. With a pull CDN, the edge fetches from your origin on the first miss and caches according to Cache-Control; with a push CDN you upload content ahead of time. Static assets get long TTLs with versioned file names; HTML and API responses get short TTLs or are passed through. CDNs also terminate TLS close to the user, absorb DDoS traffic, apply WAF rules, and can run small functions at the edge (redirects, A/B bucketing, auth token checks). Origin shielding (one regional cache in front of the origin) stops every PoP from hitting the origin on a miss.

A reverse proxy (Nginx, Envoy, HAProxy) sits in front of your servers: TLS termination, compression, routing by host/path, request buffering (protects app servers from slow clients), caching, rate limiting, retries and health-checked load balancing. A forward proxy sits in front of clients (corporate egress, outbound allow-lists, outgoing request logging).

An API gateway is a reverse proxy specialized for APIs: authentication (validate JWT or API keys), per-client quotas, request validation, routing to services, protocol translation (REST to gRPC), and API analytics. A service mesh handles the same concerns between internal services with sidecar proxies.

Typical layering: DNS → CDN/WAF → regional L4 load balancer → L7 gateway → services → caches and databases. Draw it once early in a design and refer back to it.

sections.title: Load balancer algorithms and when each fits

blocks.body:
Round robin: equal servers, similar requests. Weighted round robin: mixed instance sizes. Least connections / least outstanding requests: long or uneven requests (uploads, streaming). Power of two choices: pick two random servers, send to the less loaded; nearly as good as least-connections with no global state. Consistent hashing on a key: cache affinity (same user → same cache node) at the cost of uneven load for hot keys.

Health checks remove dead backends; connection draining lets in-flight requests finish during deploys. The balancer itself is made redundant with an active-passive pair sharing a virtual IP, or several balancers behind DNS / anycast.

architecture.name: Shortener API
architecture.role: Accepts a long URL, takes the next id from a local block, scrambles it, encodes it in base62 and inserts the row with a unique constraint.
architecture.scale: About 39 writes a second on average (100 million a month). A few stateless servers are plenty; the id block means one allocator call per 1,000 writes.
architecture.failure: If one server dies, the others carry on and the unused part of its block (up to 999 ids) is wasted, which is nothing against 3.5 trillion codes.

architecture.name: Id block allocator
architecture.role: Hands each API server a block of 1,000 consecutive ids in one call, so no network call is needed per URL.
architecture.scale: One row or ZooKeeper counter that is called once per 1,000 writes across the fleet. Easily one small replicated node.
architecture.failure: If it is down, servers keep writing until their block runs out: about 250 seconds at 4 ids a second each. Redirects are not affected. A 10,000-id block stretches that to 40 minutes.

architecture.name: URL store
architecture.role: Holds code, long URL, owner, expiry and flags. Every access is by code, so it shards by hash of the code.
architecture.scale: 100 million rows a month at about 500 bytes is 6 billion rows and 3 TB over five years. Spread over a few shards with replicas.
architecture.failure: A down shard fails only its own codes, and a replica can be promoted. The unique constraint on the code is the final guard against duplicates.

architecture.name: Redis cache
architecture.role: Answers redirects from memory and falls back to the store on a miss. Each entry lives for the smaller of an hour and the time to expiry.
architecture.scale: The hottest 1 percent (1 million links) at about 120 bytes is roughly 120 MB. Expect a hit ratio above 90 percent, cutting 20,000 reads a second at peak to under 2,000.
architecture.failure: If a node dies, misses jump about 10 times and fall on the database. Use a replicated cluster, warm the replacement and coalesce concurrent misses for the same code.

architecture.name: Click pipeline (Kafka and aggregator)
architecture.role: The redirect service publishes a click event without waiting, and an aggregator counts clicks per link.
architecture.scale: Around 4,000 events a second on average, 20,000 at peak, each a few dozen bytes. Small for a Kafka topic.
architecture.failure: If Kafka is down, drop or buffer events locally. A few lost counts are acceptable; a slow redirect is not.

blocks.body: Options: (1) hash the URL (MD5 → first 7 chars) and handle collisions by retrying with a salt, which also dedupes identical URLs; (2) a counter/ID service handing out ranges to each app server, base62-encoded: no collisions, but codes are guessable (shuffle bits or add a random component if that matters); (3) pre-generate random codes into a key pool table and hand them out. Range-based counters are the simplest robust answer.

301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect, cutting load but losing click analytics and the ability to change the target. 302 (temporary) sends every click through you. Most shorteners use 302 for analytics.
A viral link is a hot key: the cache absorbs it (plus CDN). Expired links: check expires_at on read and delete lazily, with a background cleanup job.

Start from the requirements, because they set every other choice. 100 million new URLs a month is 100,000,000 / (30 x 86,400) = about 39 writes a second on average. With a read-to-write ratio of 100 to 1, that is about 3,900 redirects a second on average, and a peak of perhaps 5 times the average, about 20,000 a second. Neither number is large: one well-tuned Redis node handles 100,000 operations a second, and a few application servers handle 20,000 redirects. The design is not about raw throughput. It is about three other things: a code that never collides, a cache that absorbs the hot links, and a read path that stays up when parts of the system are down.

Storage: a row holds the code (7 bytes), the long URL (average perhaps 100 bytes, with 2,000 as the practical limit), a user id, two timestamps and some flags. Budgeting 500 bytes per row, 100 million rows a month for five years is 6 billion rows and 3 TB. That fits on a small cluster of ordinary database machines, and since every access is by the code, the data shards cleanly by code.

How long must the code be? With 62 characters (digits, lower case, upper case), 6 characters give 62^6 = 56.8 billion codes and 7 characters give 62^7 = 3.5 trillion. Six billion URLs over five years fits in 6 characters with room to spare, but 7 leaves a thousandfold margin and makes guessing codes harder. The demo below confirms the figure: it prints 3,521,614,606,208 for the number of 7-character codes.

The cache size follows from how links are used. Link popularity is very skewed: a small share of links gets most of the clicks. If the hottest 1 percent of 100 million links, one million of them, is cached at about 120 bytes each (code plus URL plus overhead), the cache holds about 120 MB. A single Redis node can hold it, and a cache of a few gigabytes could hold far more than the working set. Expect a hit ratio above 90 percent, which cuts database reads from 20,000 a second at peak to under 2,000.

The central question is how to produce a short unique code. There are four common answers, and the right one depends on what you want to guarantee.

**Hash the URL and truncate.** Take MD5 or SHA-256 of the long URL, encode it in base62 and keep the first 7 characters. The same URL always gets the same code, which gives deduplication for free, and no coordination between servers is needed. The problem is collisions: two different URLs can share a prefix. By the birthday approximation, with N possible codes and n URLs, the expected number of colliding pairs is about n^2 / (2N). For n = 1 billion and N = 3.5 trillion, that is (10^9)^2 / (7 x 10^12), roughly 143,000 colliding pairs. So the insert must check for an existing code and, on a conflict, retry with a salt appended to the URL. That works, but every write becomes a read-then-write, and the number of retries grows as the table fills.

**A random code, checked.** Generate 7 random base62 characters, insert with a unique constraint, retry on conflict. It is simple and the codes are unguessable, but it has the same collision handling as hashing, without the deduplication benefit.

**A global counter, encoded.** Keep one counter, increment it per URL and encode the number in base62. Collisions are impossible by construction. Ids are small (the first million are at most 4 characters). The weakness is the counter itself: a single database row or ZooKeeper node taking 40 increments a second is fine, but a network call on every write is a dependency on the write path, and sequential codes let anyone enumerate every link by counting.

**A counter handed out in blocks, then scrambled.** This is the design to propose. A small allocator service hands each application server a block of, say, 1,000 consecutive ids in one call. The server hands out ids from memory with no network call and fetches a new block only when it runs out. A crashed server wastes at most the unused part of its block, up to 999 ids, which is nothing against 3.5 trillion. To stop people counting, pass each id through a reversible scramble, for example multiplication by a large odd constant modulo 2^42, which maps distinct inputs to distinct outputs and makes consecutive ids look unrelated. Then encode in base62.

The demo implements the encoder, the block allocator and the scramble. It shows that 2,500 ids need exactly 3 blocks of 1,000, that three sequential ids produce unrelated-looking codes, and that 100,000 scrambled ids are all distinct (a multiplication by an odd number modulo a power of two is a bijection, so this holds for all inputs, not only the ones tested).

The redirect status decides who owns the cache. A **301** (permanent) lets browsers and intermediaries cache the redirect forever: later clicks never reach you, which saves load but means you lose click counts, cannot change or expire the target, and cannot take a link down. A **302** (temporary) makes every click pass through your service, so analytics, expiry and abuse takedowns all work. Most shorteners use 302, or 301 with a short `Cache-Control: max-age`, and accept the load because it is small (4,000 requests a second).

A **custom alias** is a user-chosen code. It lives in the same table, and the same unique constraint protects it, so two users asking for `summer-sale` race safely: one insert wins and the other gets a conflict error. Keep the generated codes and the aliases from colliding by giving aliases a different shape (a minimum length of 8, say, or a reserved separator) and by checking reserved words such as `api` and `admin`.

**Expiry** needs two mechanisms. On read, compare `expires_at` with the current time and answer 404 or 410 when it has passed, so correctness never depends on cleanup. In the background, a sweeper deletes expired rows in small batches, using an index on the expiry time, and removes the cache entry. Put the expiry into the cache TTL too: the cache entry lives for the smaller of a default (an hour) and the time left.

**Abuse** matters more than throughput for a public shortener. Attackers use short links to hide phishing pages. Check submitted URLs against a safe-browsing list, rate-limit creation per account and per IP, allow takedown by code, and refuse to redirect to private address ranges (a server-side request forgery risk if you ever fetch the link to generate a preview).

sections.title: Failure modes and what happens to each

blocks.body:
Walk through what breaks, with numbers, because an interviewer wants to hear the system degrade gracefully.

**The cache node dies.** Every redirect becomes a database read. At the 20,000 a second peak that is a 10 times jump over the normal 2,000 misses a second. A read replica set sized for it survives; without that, the database slows and redirects time out. Mitigations: run the cache as a replicated cluster so one node loss only removes a slice, warm the replacement from the database for the hottest codes, and let the redirect service coalesce concurrent misses for the same code into one database read so a viral link does not stampede.

**The allocator is down.** Application servers keep working until their local block is used up. With 10 servers and 40 writes a second in total, each server uses about 4 ids a second, so a 1,000-id block lasts about 250 seconds, over four minutes. A longer outage means writes fail while redirects continue, which is the right priority: reads are 99 percent of the traffic. Raising the block size to 10,000 stretches the window to 40 minutes at the cost of a bigger loss per crash.

**One database shard is hot or down.** Sharding by a hash of the code spreads load evenly. If a shard is down, only the codes on it fail, unless it has a replica to promote. A single viral code is the problem a shard cannot fix, and the cache plus a CDN in front of the redirect handles it: a CDN edge can serve the redirect itself for a few seconds, which flattens a spike to a trickle at the origin.

**A region is down.** Reads are easy to serve from several regions with data replicated asynchronously, since a link created a second ago may not have arrived yet, and the right answer there is a short retry or a fallback read from the home region. Writes need one home region per code range, or an allocator per region that hands out disjoint id ranges.

**The click pipeline backs up.** Click events go to Kafka without the redirect waiting for them, so analytics lag never slows a redirect. If Kafka is unavailable, drop or buffer events locally; losing a few counts is acceptable, a slow redirect is not.
Hash-based codes dedupe but need collision handling; counters are simple but need a coordination service.
NoSQL fits the pure key-value access; relational is fine at this size with read replicas and a cache.
Read-heavy (~100:1); 7-char base62 = 3.5T codes.
Codes from a counter with range allocation (no collisions) or hash + collision check.
Redirect path: cache (Redis) → KV store; 301 cacheable vs 302 trackable.

sections.title: How do you support custom aliases?

blocks.body: Same table, insert with a uniqueness constraint on the code; reject if taken. Reserve a namespace (or length) so generated codes never collide with aliases.
301 lets browsers cache and cuts load but hides repeat clicks from analytics; 302 (or 307) keeps every click visible. Most shorteners use 302 when analytics matter.

sections.title: How do you expire links and reclaim codes?

blocks.body: Store expires_at, check it on redirect, and run a background sweeper. Don't reuse codes quickly: old links in the wild would point to new content.
Rate-limit creation per user/IP, scan destinations against malware/phishing lists, and allow takedowns.

Object-oriented design is about putting behaviour next to the data it protects and depending on abstractions. In an LLD round, interviewers judge whether your classes have clear responsibilities and whether the design bends easily when requirements change.
Keep fields private and expose behaviour, not setters: account.withdraw(amount) checks the balance itself instead of callers doing setBalance(getBalance() - x). This keeps invariants in one place.

Inheritance models 'is-a' and couples the subclass to the parent's internals; deep hierarchies get brittle. Composition ('has-a', delegating to a field) is more flexible: a Car has an Engine you can swap. Prefer composition, and use inheritance for true subtypes with shared behaviour.

Callers work with an interface (PaymentMethod) and each implementation (Card, UPI, Wallet) behaves differently behind it. This removes if/else-on-type chains, and new types are added without touching callers.

An interface is a pure contract with no state; a class can implement many, and it's the default for abstractions. An abstract class can hold shared state and partial implementation for closely related subclasses (template method). Program to interfaces.
Encapsulation: private state, public behaviour; validate in one place.
Prefer composition (has-a) over inheritance (is-a) unless substitution truly holds.
Polymorphism: call through an interface; add a class instead of an if/else branch.
Interface = capability contract; abstract class = shared partial implementation.

A BankAccount with a public balance field lets any caller make it negative. Make balance private and expose withdraw(amount) that checks the rule in one place; there's no setter. Return unmodifiable views of internal collections so callers can't add items behind your back.

In interviews, when you draw a class, say which invariant each method protects ('a slot can be occupied by at most one vehicle').

Classic trap: class Bird { fly() }, class Penguin extends Bird → Penguin.fly() throws. The hierarchy encoded a capability that not every subtype has. Composition models capabilities as parts: a Bird has a MovementStrategy (Flying, Swimming, Walking). New combinations need no new subclasses, and behaviour can change at runtime.

Use inheritance for true 'is-a' with shared invariants (ArrayList is a List), and keep hierarchies shallow.

Compile-time polymorphism (overloading): same method name with different parameter lists in one class (print(int), print(String)); the compiler picks based on static types. Runtime polymorphism (overriding): a subclass provides its own implementation of an inherited method; the JVM picks based on the object's actual class (dynamic dispatch). Overriding is what lets you replace conditionals with objects.

Overriding rules: same signature, return type the same or a subtype (covariant), can't reduce visibility, can't throw broader checked exceptions; use @Override so the compiler catches mistakes. static methods are hidden, not overridden; private methods aren't inherited. Fields aren't polymorphic.

equals and hashCode: if two objects are equal, their hash codes must match, or HashMap/HashSet break. Override both together for value objects (Money, Point, Coordinate), and keep them consistent with the fields that define identity. Prefer immutable value objects (Java records give equals/hashCode/toString for free).

Abstraction means exposing what an object does and hiding how. In Java, an interface declares a capability (Comparable, Runnable, PaymentMethod) with no state; a class can implement many. Since Java 8, interfaces can have default methods for shared behaviour, but still no instance fields. An abstract class can hold state and constructors and partially implement behaviour, but a class extends only one.

Rule of thumb: use an interface for a role that unrelated classes may play (Notifier implemented by EmailNotifier, SmsNotifier). Use an abstract class when subclasses share real state and a template of steps (an AbstractReportGenerator with generate() calling abstract fetchData() and format(): the template method pattern). Program to interfaces in fields and parameters (List<Order> rather than ArrayList<Order>) so implementations can change.

In interviews, define the interfaces first for the parts that will vary (pricing, matching, notification channels), then write concrete classes.

sections.title: Cohesion, coupling and good class boundaries

blocks.body:
High cohesion: everything in a class serves one purpose (a Ticket knows its entry time, vehicle and slot, and how long it has been open). Low coupling: classes depend on few others, through narrow interfaces, so changes stay local.

Smells in interview code: a God class (ParkingLotManager doing allocation, pricing, payments and printing), anemic models (classes with only getters/setters while all logic lives in a service), feature envy (a method mostly using another object's data, which suggests it belongs there), long parameter lists (introduce a parameter object), and primitive obsession (passing raw strings and ints for money, ids, statuses instead of types and enums).

Law of Demeter: talk to your direct collaborators, not their internals (lot.getFloor(2).getSlots().get(5).park(car) leaks structure; prefer lot.park(car) delegating down). Following these keeps the class diagram you draw in an interview clean and easy to extend.
Composition vs inheritance: give a case where inheritance goes wrong.
Interface vs abstract class in Java?

Hourly pricing that differs by vehicle type; pluggable pricing.

sections.title: What to clarify before drawing anything

blocks.body:
Parking lot is the most common LLD question because it is small enough to finish and rich enough to show judgement. The first five minutes decide the rest, so spend them asking.

Ask about the vehicles: which types exist, and does a bigger vehicle ever fit in a bigger spot? (Yes in our design: a car may use a large spot if no medium one is free, but never the other way round.) Ask about the building: one floor or many, one entrance or several. Several entrances is the quiet requirement that forces you to think about concurrency, so get it said out loud. Ask about money: is the price per hour, per day, or flat, and does it differ by vehicle type? Ask what happens when the lot is full: reject, or queue? And ask what is out of scope: CCTV and number plate recognition can be waved away if the interviewer agrees.

Then ask which follow-ups are in play. Electric vehicle chargers, reservations, paying at the exit, lost tickets, an operator report and several lots are the usual ones, and this solution includes all of them. Build the core first (enter, exit, fee), get it working, and only then add each follow-up as a separate step. An interviewer who sees the core finished and then extended without a rewrite learns far more about you than one who watches you design everything at once.

Write the agreed requirements as four or five short lines on the board. Everything you build afterwards should trace back to one of those lines, and when the interviewer later says "now make it support electric vehicle charging" you can point at the line that changes.

sections.title: The entities and why they look like this

blocks.body:
Underline the nouns in the requirements: vehicle, spot, floor, ticket, lot, price, reservation, payment, receipt. That list is a starting point, not a design, and the skill is deciding which nouns deserve a class.

Vehicle becomes a record with a plate, a type and a flag for whether it needs a charger. It has no behaviour except computing the smallest spot it fits, and it never changes, so a record is exactly right. A second constructor keeps the common case short: new Vehicle("KA01", CAR) is a petrol car, Vehicle.ev("KA02", CAR) is an electric one. We deliberately do not create Car, Bike and Truck subclasses. They would differ only in one number, and a new vehicle type would then mean a new class instead of a new enum constant.

Spot is the only mutable domain object. It has two mutable facts: who is parked there, and which plate (if any) holds it until a given time. Everything else (id, floor, size, whether it has a charger) is final. Because the spot owns its own state, it can also own the lock for that state, and that is what lets a gate and a booking app race for the same spot without any lock on the lot. This is the key idea in the concurrency section.

Floor is a noun in the requirements but not a class here. A floor would be a list of spots with no behaviour of its own, so we store the floor number on each spot and sort by it when we want the nearest one. If floors later get behaviour (a display per floor, a barrier per floor) then a Floor class earns its place; until then it is ceremony. Saying this out loud in an interview is a strength: you are showing that you add classes for reasons.

Ticket, Reservation and Receipt are records. A ticket links the vehicle, the spot and the entry time. A reservation links a plate to a spot until a deadline. A receipt is what the customer gets back from a successful checkout: fee, payment method and change. ParkingLot is the facade that enforces the rules of entry, reservation and exit, and is the only class a caller needs. Garage sits above it and only routes.

sections.title: Patterns used, and the ones we rejected

blocks.body:
Strategy appears three times. SpotAllocationStrategy decides where to park, PricingStrategy decides what it costs, and PaymentProcessor decides how the customer pays. All three are things the business will change (park near the lift, charge more at weekends, add a new card network), and Strategy lets them change without touching ParkingLot.

Decorator appears three times as well, and it is the pattern that carries the follow-ups. DailyCapPricing wraps any pricing rule and limits it to a daily maximum. ChargingSurcharge wraps any pricing rule and adds a per-hour fee when the spot has a charger. EvAwareStrategy wraps any allocation strategy and reorders its candidates so that electric vehicles see chargers first and petrol cars see them last. Each decorator implements the same interface as the thing it wraps, so the lot never learns how many are stacked, and stacking them in Main is one line each.

Observer appears once: OccupancyListener. The display board at the entrance wants to know when counts change, and the lot should not know that a display board exists. Today there is one listener that stores the latest counts. Tomorrow it could be a mobile app feed.

Facade and Adapter are in there quietly. ParkingLot is a facade over spots, tickets, pricing and payment. CardPayment is an adapter: it turns the lot's question "charge this many cents" into the card network's question "authorize this card for this amount", and the network itself sits behind the small CardGateway interface so tests can fake it.

Patterns we rejected on purpose. Singleton for the lot: it hides a dependency, makes tests share state, and gains nothing, because Main simply creates one lot and passes it around. Factory for tickets: creating a ticket is one line and has no variation, so a factory would only be a place to hide that line. Inheritance for vehicles, for the reason above. A full State pattern for spots: a spot has three situations (free, held, occupied), but a failed move changes nothing and two fields describe all of them, so a state class per situation would be more code than the logic it replaces. Naming what you did not use, and why, earns more than listing patterns you did.

sections.title: The main flow, step by step

blocks.body:
Entry. The caller invokes enter(vehicle). The lot first adds the plate to a set of plates currently inside; if the add fails, the same vehicle is already in the building and the request is rejected. Next it looks for a reservation for this plate and removes it from the map in the same step. If there is one and it has not expired, the lot tries to park the vehicle in the spot that was kept for it. Otherwise (no reservation, an expired one, or a hold that somehow failed) the allocation strategy returns the free spots that fit, ordered by preference, and the lot walks that list and calls tryPark on each spot until one succeeds. The first success creates a ticket with a sequence number and the current time from the injected clock, stores it in the active map, and notifies listeners. If the list runs out, the lot throws LotFullException and the plate is removed from the set so the driver can come back later.

Reservation. The caller invokes reserve(vehicle, hold). The lot asks the same allocation strategy for candidates and calls tryHold on each until one accepts, then stores the reservation by plate. The whole step runs inside ConcurrentHashMap.compute, so two requests for the same plate cannot both succeed. Someone else's tryPark on a held spot returns false until the deadline passes, which is how the spot stays kept without any timer.

Checkout. The caller invokes checkout(ticketId, payment). The lot removes the ticket from the active map; the removal is the single moment that decides whether the ticket is valid, so a second scan of the same ticket finds nothing and is rejected. Then the pricing strategy computes the fee from the ticket and the current time, and the payment processor is asked to charge that amount. If the payment is declined the ticket is put back, so the customer can try another way to pay. If it is approved, the fee is added to the revenue counters, the spot is released, the plate leaves the set, listeners are notified and a Receipt is returned. The old exit(ticketId) still exists for flows where the money was settled elsewhere: it is checkout with a processor that always approves.

Run Main to see it. The first half is the original scenario: a car, a bike and a truck enter and are assigned F0-M0, F0-S0 and F0-L0, a car that stayed 150 minutes pays for three hours, the same bike plate is turned away because it is already inside, and a third truck is rejected when both large spots are taken. The second half uses a small bay with one charger: a petrol car is kept off the charger, an electric car gets it, a reservation keeps the last spot from a stranger and gives it to its owner ten minutes later, a short cash payment is declined and then a card payment works, the electric car pays the charging surcharge, a lost ticket costs the flat penalty, and the report adds the three payments up. The third part puts two lots behind one garage.

Chargers need two small additions and no change to the lot. The spot gets a final flag, isEv, and the pricing and allocation each get a decorator. EvAwareStrategy splits the inner strategy's candidates into two groups, those whose charger flag matches the vehicle and those that do not, and returns the first group followed by the second. So an electric car is offered chargers first and plain spots after, and a petrol car the other way round. An electric car is allowed to take a plain spot because turning it away from a lot with free spots would be worse than not charging it. ChargingSurcharge adds a per-started-hour fee when the ticket's spot has a charger, and because it is a decorator, "hourly plus charging" and "daily cap on hourly plus charging" are one line each in Main. The order of wrapping matters and is worth a sentence in an interview: capping outside the surcharge caps the total, capping inside it caps only the parking.

Reservations are the one follow-up that changes the model, because a spot is no longer simply free or taken. The design keeps the change inside Spot. A spot has an optional hold: a plate and a deadline. tryPark refuses any vehicle whose plate is not the holder while the deadline is in the future, and tryHold refuses when the spot is occupied or held by someone else. Both read and write under the spot's own lock, which is the whole point: a booking app and a gate that want the same spot meet at the spot, and one of them wins. A hold needs no cleanup job, because a deadline in the past simply stops mattering. freeCounts counts a held spot as unavailable, so the display board does not promise a spot that is kept for someone else.

The lot stores reservations by plate in a concurrent map. reserve runs inside compute for that plate, which makes "one reservation per plate" a property of the map and not a hope. enter removes the reservation with the same atomic step, so a reservation can be used only once, and an expired one is cleared and the vehicle parks like anyone else.

The Garage is the smallest design in the project and the one that shows restraint. It holds named lots in a fixed order and tries each in turn until one accepts the vehicle. It keeps its own set of plates because each lot only knows about its own, and one vehicle must not be inside two lots. Its ticket id is the lot name, a slash and the lot's ticket id, so every lot can number its tickets from one. ParkingLot does not know the garage exists. If the rule were "closest lot to the driver" or "emptiest lot", only the order in which the garage tries the lots would change.

sections.title: Payment, lost tickets and the operator report

blocks.body:
Payment is a Strategy called PaymentProcessor with one method, charge(amountCents), that returns a PaymentResult: approved or declined, the method name, the change and a note. CashPayment compares the money handed over with the fee and returns the change. CardPayment asks a CardGateway to authorize the amount and reports the answer. The lot never imports a card SDK, and the tests pass a lambda as the gateway, so a decline is one line to set up. A processor that throws is treated like a decline for the ticket's sake: the ticket is put back and the exception is rethrown, so a crash in the payment code can never swallow a ticket.

Why does the ticket leave the map before payment, and come back after a decline? Because the removal is what makes only one caller own the checkout at a time. While one caller is mid-payment, a second scan of the same ticket gets InvalidTicketException instead of racing the first. If the first caller fails to pay, the ticket returns and the customer, or the next try, can pay again. The cost is a short window where a valid ticket looks invalid. That is a deliberate trade: the alternative, a per-ticket lock held during a network call, would block a gate on a slow card terminal.

A lost ticket is found by plate. The lot scans the active tickets for the plate, removes that ticket (if the removal fails, another gate got it first and the request is rejected), and charges the larger of the real fee and a flat penalty. A short stay pays the penalty, which is the point, and a very long stay pays what it actually cost, so losing a ticket never makes parking cheaper. A real lot would also check the driver's identity against the registration. That is out of scope here and worth saying so.

The report is for the operator. The lot keeps LongAdder counters for revenue and completed stays and one per vehicle type, all updated only after an approved payment, so a declined attempt adds nothing. LotReport is an immutable snapshot: revenue, stays, open tickets, revenue by type and the free spots at that moment. The Garage report sums the lots and keeps each lot's own report next to the total. LongAdder is chosen because many gates add at once and almost nobody reads, which is the case it is built for.

Money is a long in the smallest unit. Doubles cannot represent 0.10 exactly, and the errors show up as a missing cent on a receipt. Whenever an interviewer sees a double next to a price, they note it.

Time comes from a Clock that is passed in. The lot never calls Instant.now(), so a test can use MutableClock, advance it by 61 minutes, and assert the fee without sleeping. The same clock drives reservation deadlines: the test that reserves a spot for 30 minutes, advances 31 and sees the spot free again takes no time at all. This is the cheapest improvement you can make to a design and it is worth doing in every problem that involves time.

The tests run without JUnit so you can copy the files into a folder and run them. They cover the core: the smallest fitting spot wins; a full lot rejects the next vehicle; fees round up to whole hours (0 minutes costs one hour, 60 minutes one hour, 61 minutes two hours); the daily cap; a plate cannot enter twice; a ticket cannot be redeemed twice; and one hundred cars racing for twenty spots yields exactly twenty tickets. They also cover the follow-ups: an electric car is offered the charger first and a petrol car is not; the charging surcharge counts started hours; a reserved spot is kept for its plate, a stranger is turned away and the holder gets it; a reservation expires and can be cancelled; one plate cannot hold two reservations; a declined payment keeps the ticket valid and a later card payment succeeds; cash returns change; a lost ticket pays the larger of the penalty and the real fee; the report adds up by vehicle type; the garage overflows to its second lot and refuses one plate in two lots; and fifty plates racing for ten spots make exactly ten reservations on ten different spots.

Two of these tests are the ones that fail if you take a shortcut. The hundred-cars test fails if you replace tryPark with a check and then a write, and the fifty-plates test fails if you check a spot's hold outside its lock. Showing an interviewer a test that your own design makes pass, and the broken version makes fail, is a strong move.

Each extension below should touch as little code as possible, and saying which classes change is the answer the interviewer wants. The first few are already built here, so you can point at the code.

A new vehicle type, such as a van: add a constant to VehicleType, add its case in Vehicle.minSize, add its rate to the pricing map. Nothing else changes.

Electric vehicle charging spots: built. The capability is a flag on Spot, the allocation change is EvAwareStrategy, the pricing change is ChargingSurcharge. If chargers need energy-based pricing, ChargingSurcharge is the class to replace, and it needs the kilowatt hours from somewhere, which is a new input to the ticket or a meter service.

Reservations: built, inside Spot. If reservations must survive a restart, Reservation becomes a stored entity and the hold is rebuilt from it at start-up.

Payment, lost tickets and reports: built. If receipts must be emailed or printed, that is an observer on checkout, not a change to checkout. If refunds are needed, a Receipt is the thing to refund against, which is why it carries the ticket id and the method.

Several lots: built as Garage. A smarter routing rule changes only the order in which Garage tries lots.

Persistence: replace the in-memory map of active tickets with a repository interface. The lot should not care whether tickets live in memory or in a database. If the lot must survive a restart, spots, tickets and reservations need to be reloaded consistently, and the write that matters most is the ticket, written before the barrier opens.

Still open and worth naming: valet and handicapped spots (a capability on Spot, like the charger), monthly passes (a PaymentProcessor or a PricingStrategy that recognises the plate), and faster allocation, where a free list per size ordered by floor replaces the scan.

sections.title: What interviewers probe, and short answers

blocks.body:
Why is there no global lock? Because the contention is per spot, not per lot. A global lock makes entries from several gates queue behind each other, while per-spot locking lets them proceed in parallel and only serialises two gates that want the same spot.

What if the strategy returns a spot that another gate takes first? That is why the strategy returns a list and the lot calls tryPark on each: a failed tryPark just moves to the next candidate. The same holds for a spot that gets reserved between listing and parking: tryPark refuses it and the lot moves on.

How does a reservation race with a gate? Both go through the spot's lock. tryHold and tryPark each check "occupied or held by someone else" and then write, as one step, so there is no moment where both can believe they won.

Why is the ticket removed from the map before computing the fee? So that the removal acts as the atomic check, making a ticket single-use even under concurrency. A declined payment puts the ticket back.

What if the payment succeeds but the process dies before the spot is released? The customer has paid and the car is still marked inside. That is the argument for writing the payment record and the release in one transaction when the lot is backed by a database, and for making release idempotent.

How do you scale this to a hundred lots? Each lot is independent, so shard by lot id. The only shared data is the plate set per lot, which stays inside the lot, and the garage's own plate set if lots share a garage.

How would you find a nearby spot faster than scanning all of them? Keep a free list per size, as a priority queue ordered by floor, so allocation is logarithmic instead of linear. We scan because the interviewer's lot has hundreds of spots, not millions, and the scan is simple; say so and offer the optimisation.

What happens if the process crashes with cars inside? In memory, you lose the tickets. State what you would persist: spots, active tickets and reservations, written before the barrier opens.

Why LongAdder for revenue? Many gates add and rarely anyone reads. LongAdder spreads the contention over cells and sums them on read, which beats a single AtomicLong under load, at the cost of a sum that is not a point-in-time snapshot while writes continue.

row.title: Snapshot Array
constraints: 0 <= snap_id < the number of snap calls so far
row.complexity: set O(1), snap O(1), get O(log k) where k is the number of changes of that index.

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-1146
pattern: design-problems
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(1) set/snap, O(log S) get time, O(length + U) space"
reviewed: false
---

cases.explanationMd: The snapshot with id 0 was taken while element 0 was 5. The later set(0,6) does not change it.

hints.bodyMd: Copying the whole array on every snapshot wastes space. What if you only recorded the moments when something changed?
Most elements do not change between snapshots, so each index can keep its own history of changes.
For each index, keep a list of snapshot id and value pairs, then binary search that list for the last entry at or before the requested snapshot.
Start every list with an entry for snapshot 0 so every index has a value. If an index is set twice within one snapshot, overwrite the last entry.

blocks.body: Design an array of integers, all 0 at the start, that can take snapshots.

set(index, val) changes one element. snap() takes a snapshot of the whole array and returns its id; the first snapshot has id 0, the next 1, and so on. get(index, snap_id) returns the value that element had when snapshot snap_id was taken.
Copying the whole array on every snap is too slow and too big. Only store what changed.

Each test gives the operations in order (the class name first, then method names) and their arguments; the expected answer has one entry per operation, with null for the constructor and for methods that return nothing.

- What is the initial value of elements in the array? (All elements start initialized to 0 at snap id 0).
- What does `snap()` return? (Returns the current `snap_id`, starting at 0 and incrementing by 1 on each call).
- Can the same index be modified multiple times between two `snap()` calls? (Yes, multiple `set` calls within the same snapshot epoch should overwrite the value for that snapshot).
- What are the scale constraints? ($length \le 50,000$, and up to $100,000$ operations in total).
- Does `get(index, snap_id)` ever ask for a `snap_id` that hasn't been taken yet? (Constraints guarantee $0 \le snap\_id < \text{total snaps taken}$).

- Basic snapshot tracking:
  - `SnapshotArray(3)`: Array of size 3 initialized to 0.
  - `set(0, 5)`
  - `snap()` $\implies$ returns snapshot id 0.
  - `set(0, 6)`
  - `get(0, 0)` $\implies$ returns 5 (value of index 0 when snapshot 0 was recorded).
  - Snapshot id 0 retains 5 even though current value of index 0 is 6.
- Multiple snaps without sets:
  - `snap()` returns 1, `snap()` returns 2.
  - `get(0, 1)` and `get(0, 2)` both return 6.

A naive implementation makes a full copy of the entire array on every `snap()` call (e.g. `vector<vector<int>> snapshots`). With `length = 50,000` and up to $50,000$ snapshots, copying the array requires $O(length)$ per `snap`, consuming up to $50,000 \times 50,000 = 2.5 \times 10^9$ integers ($\approx 10$ GB RAM), causing Memory Limit Exceeded and Time Limit Exceeded.

Most indices are not modified in every snapshot. Instead of storing a full array copy for each snapshot, record history **per index**.
- For each index $i \in [0, length - 1]$, maintain a list of pairs: `(snap_id, value)`.
- Initialized with `(0, 0)` for all indices.
- When `set(index, val)` is called, check the current `snap_id`: if the last entry for that index already matches `snap_id`, overwrite it in-place; otherwise, append `{snap_id, val}`.
- Because `snap_id` values grow monotonically, each index's history list is inherently sorted by `snap_id`.
- `get(index, snap_id)` simply binary searches the index's history list for the latest entry with $id \le snap\_id$.

1. Maintain:
   - `int snaps = 0`: tracks the current snapshot counter.
   - `vector<vector<pair<int, int>>> history`: initialized to size `length`, where each index holds `vector<pair<int, int>>{{0, 0}}`.
2. Operation `set(index, val)`:
   - Access `h = history[index]`.
   - If `h.back().first == snaps`, overwrite `h.back().second = val`.
   - Else, append `{snaps, val}`.
3. Operation `snap()`:
   - Return `snaps++`.
4. Operation `get(index, snap_id)`:
   - Access `h = history[index]`.
   - Perform an upper-bound binary search to find the first entry with `snap_id_entry > snap_id`.
   - The valid snapshot state is the element right before it: `h[lo - 1].second`.

Complexity:
- Time: `set` takes $O(1)$ time. `snap` takes $O(1)$ time. `get` takes $O(\log S)$ time where $S$ is the number of distinct snapshot updates applied to that specific index.
- Space: $O(length + U)$ total space where $U$ is the number of distinct `set` updates across different snapshot epochs.
Keep a counter of snapshots taken so far. For every index keep a list of (snap id, value) pairs, starting with (0, 0).

blocks.body: set writes at the current snap id: if the last pair of that index already has this id, overwrite its value, otherwise append a new pair. snap returns the counter and adds one to it.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: get binary searches the index's list for the last pair with an id at most snap_id and returns its value.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `history(length, vector<pair<int, int>>{{0, 0}})`: initializes all cells to 0 at snap 0 so binary search always finds a valid predecessor.
- `if (h.back().first == snaps) h.back().second = val;`: coalesces multiple sets in the same epoch to avoid redundant history nodes.
- `int snap() { return snaps++; }`: snapshot generation runs in pure $O(1)$ without touching the array.
- `int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (h[mid].first <= snap_id) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid;`: upper-bound binary search.
- `return h[lo - 1].second;`: returns the value active at `snap_id`.

- Snap before any set: `SnapshotArray(1)`, `snap()` returns 0. `get(0, 0)` searches `[(0, 0)]`, returns 0.
- Overwrite in same snap: `set(0, 4)`, `set(0, 5)`, `set(0, 6)`. Index 0 has only one entry `(0, 6)`. `snap()` returns 0. `get(0, 0)` returns 6.
- Non-consecutive sets: Set index 0 at snap 0 and snap 5. Queries for snaps 1, 2, 3, 4 return the snap 0 value via `lo - 1`.

- What if we need to rollback / revert to a previous snapshot?
  Pop historical entries with `snap_id > target_snap`, or create a new snapshot that points backwards.
- How does this relate to persistent data structures?
  This is a partially persistent array. Full persistence (branching snapshots) can be implemented using a persistent segment tree with path copying in $O(\log n)$ per update.
- What if `length` was $10^9$ and queries were sparse?
  Replace the outer `vector` with an `unordered_map<int, vector<pair<int, int>>>` to support sparse indices.

- Copying the full array in `snap()`, triggering memory limit exceeded.
- Forgetting to overwrite `h.back()` when multiple sets happen in the same snapshot epoch, creating duplicate snap ids and corrupting binary search.
- Forgetting the initial `(0, 0)` baseline, causing binary search out-of-bounds errors on indices that were never explicitly updated.

- Partially persistent data structures.
- Copy-on-write and delta-compression caching strategies.

constraints: At most 200000 calls to get and put

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-146
pattern: lru--lfu-design
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(1) time per op, O(capacity) space"
reviewed: false
---

cases.explanationMd: get(1) makes key 1 the most recent, so put(3,3) throws out key 2. Then put(4,4) throws out key 1.
With room for one pair, every new key replaces the old one.

hints.bodyMd: Two things must be fast here: finding a key, and knowing which key was used longest ago. Can one structure do both?
A lookup table finds any key quickly but does not know the order. A chain of entries keeps the order, and you can reach any entry in it directly if you hold a pointer to it.
Pair a hash map from key to its place in a doubly linked list ordered by recency. Move an entry to the front on each use, and evict from the back.
On a put of an existing key, update the value and move that entry to the front instead of adding a second entry.

blocks.body: Design a cache that holds at most capacity key-value pairs and throws out the least recently used pair when it is full.

get(key) returns the value stored for key, or -1 if there is none. put(key, value) stores the pair; if the key is already there it only changes its value. When a put would take the cache over capacity, the pair that was used longest ago is removed first. Both get and put count as using a key. Both must run in O(1) on average.

Each test gives the operations in order (the class name first, then method names) and their arguments; the expected answer has one entry per operation, with null for the constructor and for methods that return nothing.

- What operations must be supported? (`get(key)` returning value or -1, and `put(key, value)` inserting or updating).
- What defines "least recently used"? (Both `get` and `put` count as using a key; eviction targets the key accessed longest ago).
- What is the cache capacity? ($1 \le capacity \le 3000$).
- What should happen if `put` updates an existing key when capacity is full? (The value is updated and marked most recent, but no eviction occurs since cache size does not increase).
- What are the time complexity requirements? (Both `get` and `put` must run in strict $O(1)$ average time).

- Eviction order: `capacity = 2`.
  - `put(1, 1)`, `put(2, 2)`: Cache holds `[2, 1]` (2 is most recent).
  - `get(1)`: Returns 1, moves 1 to most recent $\implies [1, 2]$.
  - `put(3, 3)`: Cache exceeds capacity; evicts least recently used (2). Cache now holds `[3, 1]`.
  - `get(2)`: Key 2 was evicted; returns -1.
- Update existing key: `put(1, 10)` on existing key 1 updates value to 10 and moves 1 to front without evicting anything.

A naive approach uses an array or list of pairs `(key, value)` with timestamps. On each `get(key)`, iterate through the list to find the key and update its timestamp in $O(n)$ time. On each `put`, scan the list to update an existing key, or scan to find the minimum timestamp when at capacity, which takes $O(n)$ time. With up to $2 \cdot 10^5$ operations, $O(n)$ per call results in $O(n \cdot q) \approx 6 \times 10^8$ operations, failing the $O(1)$ requirement.

To achieve $O(1)$ time for both lookups and recency reordering:
1. A **hash map** provides $O(1)$ key-to-node lookup.
2. A **doubly linked list** allows $O(1)$ node insertion, removal, and movement to the front (most recent) or back (least recent), provided we already have a pointer to the node.
By combining a hash map pointing to doubly linked list nodes (or using `std::list::iterator` in C++), accessing a node via the map allows us to splice/unlink it and move it to the head in $O(1)$, while eviction simply drops the node preceding the dummy tail.

1. Maintain:
   - An integer `cap` for maximum capacity.
   - A doubly linked list of pairs `(key, value)` ordered from most recently used (head) to least recently used (tail).
   - A hash map `where` mapping each `key` to its corresponding iterator/node in the list.
2. Operation `get(key)`:
   - Look up `key` in `where`. If absent, return -1.
   - Node exists: move it to the front of the list (mark most recently used).
   - Return the node's value.
3. Operation `put(key, value)`:
   - Look up `key` in `where`.
   - If present: update its value, move the node to the front of the list, and return.
   - If absent:
     - If the list size equals `cap`:
       - Evict the least recently used element at the back (`items.back()`).
       - Erase its key from the hash map `where`.
       - Pop the node from the back of the list.
     - Insert a new `(key, value)` node at the front of the list.
     - Record `where[key] = items.begin()`.

Complexity:
- Time: $O(1)$ average time per `get` and `put` call. Hash map operations take $O(1)$ average time, and doubly linked list pointer updates take strictly $O(1)$.
- Space: $O(\text{capacity})$ auxiliary space to store at most `capacity` nodes and hash map entries.
Keep a doubly linked list of pairs ordered from most recently used (front) to least recently used (back), and a hash map from key to the list node.

In the reference implementation:
- `list<pair<int, int>> items;`: maintains access ordering from front (MRU) to back (LRU).
- `unordered_map<int, list<pair<int, int>>::iterator> where;`: provides $O(1)$ iterator access given a key.
- `items.splice(items.begin(), items, it->second);`: unlinks and splices the existing node to the front in $O(1)$ without memory reallocation.

- How does Python's `collections.OrderedDict` implement this?

Therefore, the character immediately following `c[0]` is obtained by adding 1 to its character code:

This computes the exact successor in a single CPU instruction without any array or string lookups.

2. Compute the successor character by adding 1: `next_ch = (char)(ch + 1)`.
3. Construct a 1-character string from `next_ch` and return it.

blocks.body: You have a list of whole numbers on a blackboard. In one move, if every number on the board is even, you may replace each number by half of it. Return the largest number of moves you can make.

If a number is odd you cannot move any more. A board that never runs out of moves cannot happen because every number is positive. Written for this app from the AtCoder task of the same name (linked above); the original reads from standard input, here you write a function.

- What operation is performed on the array in each step? (If every number in the array is even, replace each number with its half; otherwise, the process halts).
- What should be returned? (The maximum number of simultaneous halving operations performed before at least one number becomes odd).
- What are the constraints on array length and elements? (`1 <= a.length <= 200` and each element $1 \le a[i] \le 10^9$).
- Can any element start as odd? (Yes, if any initial element is odd, zero moves can be made; the function returns 0).
- Are elements guaranteed to be strictly positive? (Yes, $a[i] \ge 1$, so numbers never reach 0).

- Standard case: `a = [8, 12, 40]`.
  - Initial: all even. Halve once $\to [4, 6, 20]$ (1 move).
  - Second step: all even. Halve again $\to [2, 3, 10]$ (2 moves).
  - Third step: 3 is odd, so halving cannot continue. Total moves = 2.
- Starts with odd: `a = [5, 6, 8, 10]`. Element 5 is odd from the start. Returns 0.
- Single power of two: `a = [536870912]`. $536870912 = 2^{29}$. Can be halved 29 times until reaching 1. Returns 29.

A direct simulation repeatedly scans the array in a `while` loop. In each round, it iterates through all $n$ numbers to verify if all are even. If true, it divides all $n$ numbers by 2 in-place and increments a move counter. If any odd number is found, it terminates and returns the counter. Because numbers are bounded by $10^9 < 2^{30}$, each number can be halved at most 30 times. The simulation runs at most 30 rounds of size $n$, running in $O(30n)$ time. While fast enough for $n \le 200$, modifying the array across rounds is unnecessary.

The entire array halts as soon as any single element becomes odd. An integer $x$ can be halved as many times as the exponent of 2 in its prime factorization (or the number of trailing zero bits in its binary representation, $\nu_2(x)$). Because every halving step halves all elements simultaneously, the total number of operations possible is strictly constrained by the element that runs out of factors of 2 first. Therefore, the answer is simply the minimum count of factors of 2 across all elements: $\min_{x \in a} \nu_2(x)$.

1. Initialize a variable `best` to a large number (e.g., 100, since no 32-bit positive integer has more than 30 factors of 2).
2. For each number `x` in the array `a`:
   a. Count how many times `x` can be divided by 2:
      - Initialize `c = 0`.
      - While `x % 2 == 0`: divide `x /= 2` and increment `c`.
   b. Update `best = min(best, c)`.
   c. (Optional early exit): If `best == 0`, return 0 immediately.
3. Return `best`.

Complexity:
- Time: `O(n log max)` where $n$ is the number of elements and $\log(\max) \le 30$. Each number is divided by 2 at most 30 times, requiring at most $200 \times 30 = 6,000$ operations.
- Space: `O(1)` auxiliary space because we only maintain scalar loop variables without allocating additional memory or modifying the input array.
Count how many times each number can be divided by 2 (its factors of two) and return the minimum over all numbers. The board allows exactly that many moves.

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `int best = 100;`: establishes an upper bound sentinel that will be minimized.
- `for (int x : a)`: examines each element in the input list independently.
- `while (x % 2 == 0) { x /= 2; c++; }`: extracts the 2-adic valuation $\nu_2(x)$ by repeatedly halving until an odd quotient is reached.
- `best = min(best, c);`: keeps track of the element that limits the maximum halving depth of the array.
- `return best;`: returns the bottleneck operation count.

- Can we count the trailing zeros in $O(1)$ per element using bitwise intrinsics?
  Yes, using `__builtin_ctz(x)` in C++ (Count Trailing Zeros) or `Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros(x)` in Java. This computes $\nu_2(x)$ in a single CPU instruction, reducing the runtime to $O(n)$.
- What if we compute the bitwise OR of all elements first?
  The operation $\nu_2(\text{bit\_or}_{i} a[i])$ equals the minimum number of trailing zeros among all $a[i]$. Folding the entire array into a single cumulative bitwise OR in $O(n)$ and counting trailing zeros gives the exact answer with zero division operations.

- Modifying the original input array when it may be needed by the caller.

blocks.body: Alice and Bob play with cards that each show a number. They take turns, Alice first. On a turn, the player takes the card with the biggest number left. When the cards are gone, each player's score is the sum of the numbers on their cards.

Both play to maximise their own score, which means they always take the biggest card. Return Alice's score minus Bob's score. Written for this app from the AtCoder task of the same name (linked above); the original reads from standard input, here you write a function.

- Who moves first and how do turns alternate? (Alice takes the first turn, and players take turns alternately taking one card).
- What strategy do the players follow? (Both players play optimally by greedily selecting the card with the highest value remaining).
- What is the goal and return value? (Return Alice's total score minus Bob's total score).
- What are the constraints on the number of cards and their values? (`1 <= cards.length <= 100000`, and each card value is $1 \le cards[i] \le 100$).
- Can card values be duplicated? (Yes, cards can share identical values).

- Two cards: `cards = [3, 1]`. Alice takes 3, Bob takes 1. Alice's score is 3, Bob's is 1. Difference: $3 - 1 = 2$.
- Three cards: `cards = [2, 7, 4]`. Sorted descending: $[7, 4, 2]$. Alice takes 7, Bob takes 4, Alice takes 2. Alice's total is $7 + 2 = 9$, Bob's is 4. Difference: $9 - 4 = 5$.
- Identical cards: `cards = [5, 5]`. Alice takes 5, Bob takes 5. Difference: $5 - 5 = 0$.
- Single card: `cards = [1]`. Alice takes 1, Bob gets nothing. Difference: 1.

A naive simulation without sorting repeatedly scans the array $n$ times: in each of the $n$ turns, find the maximum remaining element in $O(n)$ time, add or subtract it from the score, and remove or mark it as visited. With $n \le 100,000$, finding the maximum $n$ times takes $O(n^2)$ operations ($\approx 10^{10}$ steps), which exceeds the standard time limit.

Because both players always select the card with the largest remaining value, the game sequence is entirely deterministic. If we sort the cards in descending order, Alice always receives the cards at even indices ($0, 2, 4, \dots$) and Bob always receives the cards at odd indices ($1, 3, 5, \dots$). Computing the alternating sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (-1)^i \cdot cards[i]$ directly yields the difference.

1. Sort the `cards` array in descending order.
2. Initialize an integer variable `diff = 0`.
3. Iterate through the sorted array with index `i` from 0 to $n - 1$:
   a. If `i` is even (`i % 2 == 0`), Alice took the card: add `cards[i]` to `diff`.
   b. If `i` is odd, Bob took the card: subtract `cards[i]` from `diff`.
4. Return `diff`.

Complexity:
- Time: `O(n log n)` to sort the array of $n$ elements, followed by an $O(n)$ linear alternating sum pass. For $n = 100,000$, this takes about 15 ms.
- Space: `O(1)` auxiliary space if sorting in-place (or $O(\log n)$ for recursive sorting call stack).

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `sort(cards.rbegin(), cards.rend());`: sorts the vector in descending order in $O(n \log n)$ time.
- `int diff = 0;`: tracks the net point difference between Alice and Bob.
- `for (size_t i = 0; i < cards.size(); i++)`: iterates sequentially through the cards chosen by alternating players.
- `diff += (i % 2 == 0) ? cards[i] : -cards[i];`: adds cards taken by Alice (even positions) and subtracts cards taken by Bob (odd positions).
- `return diff;`: returns the final score difference.

- Can this be solved in $O(n)$ time?
  Yes, notice that card values are constrained between 1 and 100. We can use counting sort with a frequency array of size 101 in $O(n + 100) = O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space, avoiding the $O(n \log n)$ comparison sort overhead.
- What if cards can have negative values?
  If negative cards are allowed, players would prefer not to pick negative cards if skipping is allowed. If picking remains mandatory until the deck is empty, the greedy strategy remains identical: taking the least negative card minimizes damage.

- Subtracting the scores backwards (Bob minus Alice instead of Alice minus Bob).

hints.bodyMd: Imagine pairing every takoyaki with every other one. Is there a way to get the total of all the products without listing each pair?

blocks.body: There are n takoyaki, the i-th has deliciousness d[i]. Eating two of them gives you x * y health, where x and y are their deliciousness values. Over all the pairs of different takoyaki (each pair counted once), return the total health.
Written for this app from the AtCoder problem linked above; the original reads standard input, here you write a function.

- Are we summing the product of every distinct pair of indices $(i, j)$ with $i < j$? Yes, each unordered pair of elements is counted exactly once.
- Can elements in array `d` be zero or duplicate values? Yes, deliciousness values are non-negative integers up to 100, and duplicates are treated as separate items by their distinct indices.
- How large can $n$ and the deliciousness values be? The length $n$ is up to 50, and values are up to 100.
- Can the total sum exceed standard 32-bit signed integers? With $n \le 50$ and $d[i] \le 100$, the maximum possible sum is around $\binom{50}{2} \times 100^2 \approx 1225 \times 10000 \approx 1.225 \times 10^7$, which safely fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

- Consider `d = [3, 1, 2]`.
  The pairs are $(3, 1)$, $(3, 2)$, and $(1, 2)$.
  Their products are $3 \times 1 = 3$, $3 \times 2 = 6$, and $1 \times 2 = 2$.
  The total sum of pair products is $3 + 6 + 2 = 11$.
- Consider an edge case with identical elements `d = [0, 0]`.
  There is only one pair $(0, 0)$ giving product $0$. The result is $0$.

A straightforward brute force iterates through all pairs of indices $0 \le i < j < n$ using two nested loops, accumulating $d[i] \times d[j]$ into a running total. For $n \le 50$, there are $\binom{50}{2} = 1225$ iterations, which easily passes within milliseconds. However, we can also compute the answer in a single linear pass using a clean algebraic identity.

Recall the algebraic expansion of the square of a sum:
$(\sum_{i=1}^n d[i])^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n d[i]^2 + 2 \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} d[i] \cdot d[j]$.
Rearranging terms gives:
$\sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} d[i] \cdot d[j] = \frac{(\sum_{i=1}^n d[i])^2 - \sum_{i=1}^n d[i]^2}{2}$.
Thus, by tracking the sum of elements and the sum of their squares in a single loop, we obtain the exact answer in $O(n)$ time.

1. Initialize two variables `sum = 0` and `sum_sq = 0`.
2. Iterate through each deliciousness value $x$ in array `d`:
   - Add $x$ to `sum`.
   - Add $x \times x$ to `sum_sq`.
3. Compute `(sum * sum - sum_sq) / 2` and return the result.
4. Complexity:
   - Time Complexity: $O(n)$, making a single pass over the array of size $n$.
   - Space Complexity: $O(1)$, requiring only two integer accumulators.
(d1 + d2 + ... + dn)^2 contains every square once and every pair product twice. Subtract the squares and halve the rest. A double loop over pairs is also fine for the given limits.

blocks.body:
- `int sum = 0, squares = 0;`: Maintain running totals for the first and second moments of the elements.
- `for (int x : d) { sum += x; squares += x * x; }`: Process each takoyaki's deliciousness, updating total sum and squared sum.
- `return (sum * sum - squares) / 2;`: Subtract the diagonal elements of the multiplication matrix and divide off symmetry to isolate off-diagonal pair products.

- How would you handle stream inputs where numbers arrive one at a time?

- What if the sum can overflow 32-bit integers?
  Use 64-bit integer accumulators (`long long` in C++, `long` in Java) before division.

$\text{attacks} = \lceil \frac{h}{a} \rceil$.
In integer arithmetic where standard division truncates towards zero (floor division), the ceiling division of two positive integers can be computed without floating-point conversion using:
$\lceil \frac{h}{a} \rceil = \lfloor \frac{h + a - 1}{a} \rfloor$.
This formula gives the exact answer using a single constant-time arithmetic operation.

1. Compute the ceiling division using integer arithmetic: `(h + a - 1) / a`.
2. Return the resulting integer.
3. Complexity:
   - Time Complexity: $O(1)$, exactly one addition, one subtraction, and one division.
   - Space Complexity: $O(1)$, requiring no extra storage.
The answer is ceil(h / a), computed as (h + a - 1) / a.

- `(h + a - 1) / a`: Add $(a - 1)$ to numerator to shift values so integer floor division behaves as ceiling division.

Rabin-Karp avoids full character comparisons by computing rolling hashes in O(1) time per window.

We map every string of length m to an integer using polynomial rolling hashing:
`hash(s) = sum( (s[i] - 'a' + 1) * p^i ) mod M`, where p is a prime (such as 31) and M is a large prime modulus (such as 10^9 + 9).
By precomputing prefix hashes for `text`:
The hash of substring `text[i..i+m-1]` shifted by `p^i` equals:
`(prefix_hash[i + m] - prefix_hash[i]) mod M`.
Comparing this with `(pattern_hash * p^i) mod M` checks if the hashes match in O(1) time without computing modular inverse.
Only when the hashes match do we perform an explicit character check to verify the match and avoid false positives from hash collisions.

3. Precompute powers of base `p = 31` modulo `M = 10^9 + 9`: `p_pow[k] = (p_pow[k - 1] * p) % M`.
4. Precompute prefix hashes of `text`:
   - `h[i + 1] = (h[i] + (text[i] - 'a' + 1) * p_pow[i]) % M`.
5. Compute the hash of `pattern`:
   - `h_pattern = sum((pattern[i] - 'a' + 1) * p_pow[i]) % M`.
6. For each starting position `i` from 0 to `n - m`:

   - Expected hash: `target_h = (h_pattern * p_pow[i]) % M`.

7. Return results list.

- What are the inputs? An array of $n$ applicants' desired apartment sizes, an array of $m$ available apartment sizes, and an integer tolerance $k$.
- When does an apartment match an applicant? An apartment of size $s$ matches an applicant with desired size $d$ if $d - k \le s \le d + k$.
- How many apartments can an applicant get, and how many applicants can an apartment serve? At most one applicant per apartment, and at most one apartment per applicant.
- What should be returned? The maximum number of applicants who can obtain an apartment.
- What are the constraints? $1 \le n, m \le 200000$, and $0 \le k, \text{sizes} \le 10^9$.

- Consider `applicants = [60, 45, 80, 60]`, `apartments = [30, 60, 75]`, and $k = 5$:
  - Sort applicants: `[45, 60, 60, 80]`.
  - Sort apartments: `[30, 60, 75]`.
  - Applicant 45 with apartment 30: $30 < 45 - 5 = 40$. Apartment 30 is too small for applicant 45 and will also be too small for all larger applicants. Discard apartment 30.
  - Applicant 45 with apartment 60: $60 > 45 + 5 = 50$. Apartment 60 is too large for applicant 45. Move to next applicant.
  - Applicant 60 with apartment 60: $60 - 5 \le 60 \le 60 + 5$, valid match. Increment match to 1, advance both.
  - Applicant 60 with apartment 75: $75 > 65$, too large for applicant 60. Advance applicant.
  - Applicant 80 with apartment 75: $80 - 5 \le 75 \le 80 + 5$, valid match. Increment match to 2, advance both.

A brute-force maximum bipartite matching algorithm (such as the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm or Ford-Fulkerson max flow) would construct a bipartite graph with edges between every compatible applicant and apartment. By sorting both arrays, a greedy two-pointer strategy matches the optimal maximum in $O((n + m) \log (n + m))$ time.

If we process both applicants and apartments in ascending order of size:
1. If the current apartment is strictly smaller than the applicant's lower bound ($s < d - k$), then because all subsequent applicants desire even larger sizes, this apartment can never satisfy any remaining applicant. We can safely discard this apartment and advance to the next apartment.
2. If the current apartment is strictly larger than the applicant's upper bound ($s > d + k$), then because all subsequent apartments are even larger, no remaining apartment can satisfy this applicant. We must advance to the next applicant.
3. If the apartment falls within $[d - k, d + k]$, greedily pairing them is always optimal because saving this apartment for a future applicant could only hurt or match our options, never improve them.

1. Sort `applicants` in ascending order.
2. Sort `apartments` in ascending order.
3. Initialize pointers $i = 0$ (for applicants), $j = 0$ (for apartments), and `matched = 0`.

   - Else if $\text{apartments}[j] > \text{applicants}[i] + k$, increment $i$.
   - Else: increment `matched`, increment $i$, and increment $j$.
5. Return `matched`.

- Time: $O(n \log n + m \log m)$ for sorting, followed by a linear $O(n + m)$ two-pointer sweep.
- Space: $O(1)$ auxiliary space beyond the sorting stack.

- Test case $2$: `applicants = [100, 200]`, `apartments = [10, 20]`, $k = 5$: All apartments too small $\implies 0$ matches.
- Test case $3$: `applicants = [50]`, `apartments = [50]`, $k = 0$: Exact match $\implies 1$ match.

- What if an apartment could accommodate up to $C$ applicants? We would maintain a capacity counter for each apartment before advancing pointer $j$.
- What if applicants had priorities? Priority-based greedy would require sorting by priority and using a balanced binary search tree (`multiset`) to find the smallest suitable apartment for high-priority applicants.

- Underflow in integer subtraction: If using unsigned integers, evaluating $\text{applicants}[i] - k$ when $k > \text{applicants}[i]$ causes underflow wrapping. Working with signed 64-bit integers or writing the condition as $\text{apartments}[j] + k < \text{applicants}[i]$ avoids this issue.
- Reusing an apartment or applicant: Advancing only one pointer instead of both upon a match will mistakenly allocate one entity multiple times.
- [Two Pointers Technique on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-pointer_technique)

body.title: Read the limits and turn n into a time budget
body.body: Before the story, find the largest input size. A computer does about 10^8 simple steps in a second, so the size tells you the kind of algorithm the problem expects. n = 20 invites subsets, n = 5,000 invites two nested loops, n = 10^5 invites sorting and heaps, n = 10^9 invites a formula or binary search.

body.title: Name the shape of the input
body.body: Say it in one word: array, string, linked list, tree, graph, grid, intervals, a stream of numbers, or a design with operations. The shape alone removes half of the patterns. Also note whether it is sorted and whether it can change over time.

body.title: Say exactly what is asked for
body.body: Is the output one best value, a count of ways, every solution, a yes or no, a position, an order, or a changed structure? The difference between 'the minimum' and 'all the ways' is the difference between DP or greedy and backtracking. A count of ways with a large answer usually says 'modulo 10^9 + 7'.
